title: Lawfulness is a state of affairs, not a document
paras: Start with the foundation — lawfulness is a state of affairs, not a document. A use doesn't become lawful because the council issues a certificate, or unlawful because nobody can find one; the certificate confirms a position that's already there, it doesn't create it. Something's lawful either because it never needed permission, or because it once did and the time to act has run out. Permitted is different — a positive act, someone said yes — and a use can be lawful without anyone ever approving it. I'll keep the section numbers and citations out of this; they're in the written guide.

Most people ask 'will they give me permission?' when the deciding question is 'is this already lawful?' One looks forward to the merits, the other back to facts and time. Three routes to lawful, each proved differently: it was never development — a change within a use class, or works that aren't development; or it is development but permitted in advance under permitted development rights; or it was a breach, but the enforcement period ran out and immunity hardened into lawfulness. Working out which is the first move every time.

And it's unusual ground — officer and agent ask the same question and need the same answer. No discretion, no merits. A use has either gone on long enough or it hasn't; a building was either substantially complete by a date or it wasn't. There's a right answer, so a certificate isn't about persuading anyone — it's demonstrating a fact, and once granted it fixes a position that's very hard to go behind.

title: s191 or s192: which certificate
paras: So — a section 191 or a 192? The 191 certifies what already exists: a use up and running, works already done, a breach of condition become lawful — 'I did this, is it now lawful?' The 192 certifies what's proposed — 'if I do this, will it be lawful?' One question sorts it: has it happened yet? The 191 proves a history, with dates and continuity; the 192 proves a proposition of law, that the thing needs no permission. And once work starts or a use begins you've crossed from a 192 into a 191 — a proposed certificate can't rescue what's already under way.

A lot of 192 work is use-class and materiality. A change of use is development only if it's material — fact and degree, on the character of the use — and a change within a single use class isn't development at all. Sui generis uses fall outside the classes, on ordinary principles. Intensification is the subtle one: more of the same isn't development until the increase changes the character of the use, and then it's a fresh material change — so a certificate at one intensity doesn't licence a much greater one.

The other big 192 area is permitted development, and it's a conditional grant: the permission only exists if every limitation and condition is met — one dimension over, one criterion missed, and it never covered your works. The sharpest trap is prior approval. Keenan holds that prior approval doesn't settle whether something is permitted development; it decides only the matters referred, not whether the proposal fits the class. So you can build on prior approval, express or deemed, and still have built unlawfully — the certificate is what decides it. Check for an Article 4 direction first, and remember the allowances are often cumulative, so a 191 for earlier works tells you the headroom left.

And a certificate protects exactly what it describes. Too narrow and part of what your client does goes unprotected; too wide and it won't be certified beyond the evidence. 'Commercial use' is useless; 'use of the land for the storage and distribution of building materials', with the yard and buildings on the plan, can be certified and relied on. Capture scale as well as character where intensity matters. The red line does legal work too — match it to the planning unit, take in the access, parking and yard, leave out what isn't. For a proposed certificate, describe the end state precisely and build to it — a five-person house in multiple occupation won't protect a six-person fit-out.

title: Burden and standard of proof
paras: Next, burden and standard. The burden sits entirely on the applicant, which turns ordinary development management on its head. The council doesn't investigate for you or gather evidence against you; it looks at what you filed and asks if it's enough. Confidence isn't evidence — the case is yours. So the question isn't 'is this lawful?' but 'can I prove it's lawful, and with what?'

The standard is the balance of probabilities — more likely than not, not certainty. An authority that refuses because you haven't excluded every last doubt has applied the wrong test. The refinement that wins cases, from Gabbitas and Ravensdale: where your evidence is precise and unambiguous and the council has nothing to contradict it or make it less than probable, there's no good reason to refuse — and evidence isn't rejected merely because it's uncorroborated. The authority defeats you not by demanding certainty but by putting weight on the other side — the aerial photo that doesn't fit, the enforcement visit that interrupts the period, the declarations that contradict each other.

For the officer, this is a different exercise. One question: is the matter lawful? Merits are irrelevant both ways — it doesn't matter that the use is unneighbourly or would never have been permitted, or that the circumstances are sympathetic. A refusal for insufficient information is legitimate and common, but it isn't a finding that the development is unlawful, only that the applicant hasn't proved it — curable by reapplying with better evidence. And the officer needn't give the benefit of the doubt where the doubt comes from gaps in the applicant's own case.

The mechanics. Eight weeks to determine, unless a longer period's agreed in writing. Silence past the deadline is a deemed refusal that opens the appeal — so running the clock out doesn't buy time, it hands the outcome to an inspector. The authority can grant in different terms, certifying the narrower use the evidence establishes; get the applicant's agreement, because a modified grant is a refusal in part, appealable as to the shortfall. And reasons must be given, confined to lawfulness — a refusal that strays into merits is one waiting to be overturned.

title: Evidence, continuity and gaps
paras: Now evidence, continuity and gaps. The workhorse of an existing-use case is the statutory declaration from someone with first-hand knowledge — but only as good as its content. 'Used as a workshop for years' is nearly worthless; 'started March 2009, five days a week, this is what I did, these people saw me' is worth a great deal. Around it you want documentary evidence that tips a case from arguable to certain: council tax and rates, utility bills, invoices, tenancy agreements, electoral roll. Contemporaneous documents outweigh recollection — made at the time, with no stake in an argument not yet dreamed of.

Aerial photography is often decisive, and it cuts both ways: it shows whether the structure stood in the claimed year or the ground was bare. Know where to find the historic imagery, because the other side will. The officer tests critically but fairly — probe the contradictions, check declared dates against records and imagery, weigh how close each witness really was — but never set the bar at certainty, and never reject an account just because it stands alone.

Most existing-use cases turn on a period, and most failures on a gap in it: you show the use or building across the whole span with no break that resets the clock. A short silence with a clear pattern either side can be bridged on the balance of probabilities; a long unexplained gap, or a positive sign the use stopped, cannot. A proposed case works differently — no witness statements, just a description and a legal argument: the plan, the measurements, the use-class analysis, the permitted development calculation. Precision matters even more there, because a vague proposal can't be assessed.

On a refusal you've got the appeal — against refusal, refusal in part, which takes in a grant in modified terms, or non-determination. An inspector decides the same single question, with no power to grant planning permission; beyond that lies only the High Court on a point of law. Match the procedure to the dispute: written representations where it's about what the law means on agreed facts, an inquiry where it's about whether the facts are as claimed — a disputed account of twenty years' use needs testing on oath. And front-load your evidence: material held back to appeal invites criticism and costs, and winning a disputed factual case on paper is fighting one-handed.

title: Time limits and when the clock starts
paras: Time limits, and when the clock starts. For breaches on or after the cut-off in April 2024, England now runs a single ten-year rule. The old four-year rules — operational development, and change of use to a single dwelling — survive only where the operative event falls before that line: works substantially completed, or the change of use happening, before the cut-off. The cliff edge is real: the same extension complete just either side of the cut-off is lawful in four years or in ten — a six-year swing — so which side the event falls is now the first question. Wales is unchanged; check it separately.

For operational development the clock starts at substantial completion — and Sage requires a holistic view: not whether some part was finished but whether the whole building you set out to create was substantially complete. The unfinished house never starts its clock and stays enforceable indefinitely. For a change of use, the clock starts at the material change and the use must then continue without a break — for a dwelling, actual residential use as a separate dwelling, not one merely fitted out and capable of it. Two things sit outside the ordinary limits: unauthorised works to a listed building never become immune, no period ever; and advertisements have their own ten-year, continuity-dependent code.

Once the period's run, the right is hardier than instinct suggests. A lawful use isn't lost by mere cessation — Panton and Farmer — a dormant use is still lawful and can support a certificate. It's lost only three ways: abandonment, a new planning unit, or a material change to a different use. Abandonment is objective, on four factors — physical condition, length of non-use, any intervening use, and the owner's intentions — and in Hughes thirty years of dereliction beat a professed intention to return; Hartley frames it as temporary cessation versus abandonment. A breach of condition is different — Nicholson — its lawfulness lasts only while the breach continues, so comply then breach again and a fresh clock starts. And a certificate confirming a lawful breach doesn't remove the condition; it stays on the permission.

Condition precedent is where the most damage gets done. The Whitley principle: works done in breach of a condition aren't a lawful commencement — so if the only works within the time limit breached a condition precedent, the permission was never begun, it's lapsed, and everything since is unauthorised. Hart Aggregates adds two filters: the condition must genuinely make commencement depend on it — 'no development shall take place until' — and it must go to the heart of the permission, something fundamental, not landscaping or facing bricks. Greyfort shows it biting: a levels-before-work condition was a true condition precedent, the works done in breach were no commencement, and a permission thought alive for decades had expired. So discharge conditions precedent properly before you start, and keep the evidence.

title: Concealment: Welwyn Hatfield and after
paras: Finally, concealment. In Welwyn Hatfield a barn permitted as hay storage was fitted out as a three-bedroom house from the outset and occupied undetected past the then four-year period. The Supreme Court refused on two grounds. Technical: a building that was a dwelling from the first brick never underwent a change of use to a dwelling, so that rule didn't apply. Decisive: the time limits aren't to be read to let someone profit from their own deliberate deception — the Connor principle. Fidler, the house behind straw bales, went the same way — deliberate physical concealment engaged it without any false statement on a form.

But the limits matter as much, because an officer who cries deception at every gap comes unstuck. Connor bites on deliberate, positive deception integral to the scheme — a false shell, a lie to a direct question, quiet steps to keep the authority in the dark. Ordinary silence doesn't engage it: there's no duty to announce a breach, and failing to notice something visible from the road isn't concealment. Between the poles it's fact and degree, but the touchstone is dishonest conduct, not the mere passage of unnoticed time.

Alongside the common law there's a statutory route — the planning enforcement order. The authority applies to the magistrates, within six months of sufficient knowledge, where a breach has to any extent been deliberately concealed, for an order opening a fresh year to enforce despite the expired limits. Jackson confirms the two coexist — the statute didn't displace Connor — and because 'to any extent' is a wider threshold, a scheme that might survive a Connor argument can still be caught. Concealment leaves no safe harbour in time by either route. And the taint spreads — deliberate concealment can defeat the whole certificate application, not just the concealed part of it.

And lawfulness and enforcement are two sides of one coin. A certificate can't be granted for anything contravening an enforcement notice or breach of condition notice in force — an absolute bar, at application and appeal, and pushing a certificate appeal into it is costs territory. Once a notice is served, run the lawfulness case through the enforcement appeal instead: the ground that the matters didn't occur; that they aren't a breach, where the not-development and permitted development arguments live; and that it's too late to enforce. Same burden, standard and evidence. Two points: a lawfulness ground available on that appeal and not run can be forfeited, no second bite outside it — and where the not-a-breach or too-late ground succeeds, the inspector can grant a certificate there and then, but only on an express request before the appeal is decided.
